title: Brackets and dashes for parenthesis
keyIdea: Parenthesis is extra information added inside a sentence, such as 'The oldest building (built in 1642) stands in the town square.' If you lift it out, the sentence still makes sense. Brackets, dashes and commas can all mark it, and they come in pairs, one before the extra words and one after, never mixed. The choice changes how loud the aside is: dashes make it stand out most, brackets make it quietest and commas keep it in the flow. With brackets at the end of a sentence, the full stop goes after the closing bracket.
familyTip: Take turns saying a plain sentence, such as 'Our car is red.' The other person adds a bit of extra information in the middle and says which pair of marks they would use: 'Our car – the old one – is red.' Then check it with the lift test: say it again without the extra words.

visual.caption: Is the parenthesis punctuated correctly? Drag each sentence, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The view – amazing! – made us stop.
The view – amazing!) made us stop.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: lift out extra information, bracket it, pick the pair that sets its volume, close the pair and proofread.

kid: Sometimes you add a bit of extra information in the middle of a sentence. This extra part is called parenthesis. You can lift it out and the sentence still makes sense. Try it: 'The oldest building (built in 1642) stands in the town square.' Take out the words in brackets and it still works.

Brackets, dashes and commas can all mark parenthesis. They come in pairs: one goes before the extra words and one goes after. Use the same kind of mark both times, so never start with ( and end with a dash.
Pick the pair by how loud you want the extra words to be. Dashes make them stand out. Brackets make them quiet, like a whisper. Commas keep them in the flow, like a normal part of the sentence.

If the extra words come at the very end, brackets still need both halves, and the full stop goes after the closing bracket: 'We ate at Pizza Palace (the one by the river).' With a dash or a comma at the end, the full stop takes the place of the second mark.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. English Appendix 2 of the national curriculum in England lists 'brackets, dashes or commas to indicate parenthesis' for Year 5, with parenthesis, bracket and dash as terms pupils should know. The extra information is often a relative clause (who is older than me) or a noun phrase that renames the noun before it (our head teacher).

The test that ties it together is the lift test: remove the words inside the pair and read what is left. If the sentence still works, the marks are in the right place. All three pairs are correct punctuation, so the choice is about emphasis. Dashes give the aside the most weight, brackets the least, and commas sit in between.

Common mistakes: leaving out the second comma, bracket or dash, as in 'My gran, who loves jazz plays the drums'; mixing marks, such as a dash with a closing bracket; putting the pair round words the sentence needs, so the lift test fails; putting the full stop inside a closing bracket when the bracketed words are part of the sentence; and typing a short hyphen where a dash is needed. In print a dash is a spaced en dash (–) or an unspaced em dash (—); in handwriting it is longer than a hyphen.

In the lab your child finds the part that can be lifted out of four sentences, places brackets round the aside in three more and chooses brackets, dashes or commas to match how loud five asides should be. Then they close three half-finished pairs and spot the error in six pairs of sentences.

practice.prompt: Which part of this sentence is the parenthesis? 'The Eiffel Tower, which is in Paris, is 330 metres tall.'
practice.hint: Which words could you lift out and still have a sentence?
practice.explain: 'which is in Paris' is extra information. Without it, 'The Eiffel Tower is 330 metres tall' still makes sense.

practice.prompt: A story has {n} sentences. Each one has one aside in the middle, inside brackets. How many brackets are there altogether?
practice.hint: Every aside needs a pair of brackets.
Brackets come in pairs, and you do not mix marks.
practice.explain: 'Our dog (a spaniel) barks.' has a matching pair. The second is missing a bracket, and the third mixes a dash with a bracket.

practice.prompt: A sentence has {w} words. {a} of them are inside the brackets. How many words are left after the lift test?
practice.hint: The lift test takes out every word inside the brackets.
practice.explain: {w} − {a} = {=w-a} words are left, and they should still make a sentence.

practice.prompt: You want the extra words to sound like a quiet side comment. Which pair should you use?
practice.hint: Which marks make the aside least noticeable?
practice.explain: Brackets keep the aside quiet. Dashes make it stand out, and full stops end a sentence instead of marking extra words.

pool.prompt: Which pair of marks makes the extra information stand out most?
pool.hint: Think of the marks as loud, quiet and in between.
pool.explain: Dashes make the aside stand out most. Brackets are the quietest, and commas sit in between.

pool.prompt: Where does the full stop go? 'We went to Spain (my favourite place)'
pool.hint: The bracketed words are part of this sentence.
pool.explain: The words in brackets belong to the sentence, so the full stop goes after the closing bracket: (my favourite place).

pool.prompt: Which sentence passes the lift test?
choices: The cake (a chocolate one) was huge.
The (cake a chocolate) one was huge.
(The cake) a chocolate one was huge.
pool.hint: Take out the bracketed words. Is the rest still a sentence?
pool.explain: Lift out '(a chocolate one)' and 'The cake was huge.' still works. The other two leave words that do not make sense.

pool.prompt: A paragraph has {d} asides in the middle of sentences, each marked with dashes. How many dashes does it use?
pool.hint: An aside in the middle of a sentence needs a dash on each side.

pool.prompt: Mia writes: 'My gran, who loves jazz plays the drums.' What is missing?
pool.hint: Commas for parenthesis come in pairs.
pool.explain: The aside 'who loves jazz' needs a closing comma: 'My gran, who loves jazz, plays the drums.'

pool.prompt: Which of these can NOT mark parenthesis?
pool.hint: Three kinds of pairs can mark parenthesis.
pool.explain: Brackets, dashes and commas can mark parenthesis. A question mark ends a question.

choices: The film – a comedy) was funny.
The film – a comedy – was funny.
pool.hint: Look for a pair that does not match.
pool.explain: 'The film – a comedy) was funny.' opens with a dash and closes with a bracket. Use two dashes or two brackets.

pool.prompt: A sentence has {b} words before the brackets, {i} words inside them and {f} words after. How many words are left after the lift test?
pool.hint: Only the words outside the brackets stay.
pool.explain: The {i} bracketed words go, leaving {b} + {f} = {=b+f} words.

choices: to add extra information without changing the main sentence
pool.hint: What happens to the sentence when you lift the extra words out?
pool.explain: Parenthesis adds extra information. The main sentence still works without it.
